passage:
Counsellor's note, Friday. Parul Menon, Class 10 picnic at the lake garden.
Pranav sat on the steps with his earphones in for most of the afternoon. When a group of classmates waved him over for cricket, he shrugged and looked at his phone. After two tries they stopped asking. On the bus back he told me, "Told you, ma'am. Nobody in 10B wants me around."
What I saw was a little different: they did ask, twice, and his closed face read as "not interested". I pointed that out gently and asked what he had expected before he arrived. "That they'd ignore me," he said. We agreed on a small test for Monday: say one thing to one person at lunch and notice what comes back. I will check in with him on Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Pranav tell the counsellor on the bus back?
qa.a: He said, "Told you, ma'am. Nobody in 10B wants me around."

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as he sat alone with his earphones in?
qa.a: He was likely lonely and braced for rejection, so he hid behind a bored, closed face to protect himself.

qa.q: What small test did the counsellor suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Saying one thing to one person at lunch and noticing the reply; it lets real responses, not his expectation, decide what is true.

qa.q: How might the classmates who waved him over have read Pranav's shrug?
qa.a: They probably took it as him not wanting to play and stopped asking so as not to bother him, not because they disliked him.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose expectation of rejection makes him look uninterested at a picnic, so classmates stop inviting him and his belief seems confirmed.

Sat night.
Went to Indu's birthday thing at the momo place because Ma made me. "Suraj, go, make friends," she said. Whole class was invited, so it's not like Indu actually wanted ME there.
Sat at the far end. Didn't laugh at the jokes because what's the point, they're not for me anyway. Kept checking my phone even though nobody texts me.
And guess what. Nobody talked to me the whole evening. Two hours. Proof, again.
Only weird thing: Indu came over at the start and asked if I wanted to share the chilli plate. I said "I'm fine." Later she asked if I was bored. I said "kind of."
Maybe that's why she didn't come back?
No. They just don't like me. Going to sleep.

qa.a: At the momo place.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling at the far end of the table?
qa.a: Suraj felt left out and resigned before anything happened, sure the jokes and the invitation were not really meant for Suraj.

qa.a: Say yes when someone offers, like sharing the chilli plate, and ask one question back, then notice how people respond.

qa.q: How might Indu have taken the replies "I'm fine" and "kind of"?
qa.a: Indu probably felt brushed off and thought Suraj wasn't enjoying the party, so she stopped trying rather than push.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager whose belief that classmates don't want them leads to bored, closed behaviour, so others back off and the belief seems proved.

By March, Hafsa noticed something odd in the robotics club room at her Pune college. In August she had handed Ramesh the motor driver board, half as a test, and he had burnt two fuses and asked her fifty questions. Now he was debugging other people's circuits. The other first-year, a quiet boy from Nagpur, had spent the same months labelling drawers and fetching solder, because she had thought he "wasn't ready". He still looked at her before touching anything.
Hafsa scrolled through her own messages: long replies to Ramesh, a one-line "ok" to the other boy. One of them had been given problems and feedback; the other, only chores. That evening she handed the Nagpur boy the sensor module and sat beside him while he opened the datasheet.

qa.q: What did Hafsa hand Ramesh in August?
qa.a: The motor driver board.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling as she scrolled through her own messages?
qa.a: She likely felt uncomfortable and a little guilty, seeing that her low expectations had kept the Nagpur boy stuck on chores.

qa.q: Which choice at the end could help the quieter first-year, and why?
qa.a: Giving him the sensor module and sitting beside him offers a real problem plus support, the same chance Ramesh got.

qa.q: What might it have been like for the Nagpur boy to spend months labelling drawers?
qa.a: He may have felt unimportant and unsure of his ability, so he kept waiting for permission instead of trying things.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing that the junior given real problems grew while the one kept on chores stayed stuck, because of the expectations she held.

"Minal's making the whole cold-coffee menu alone now. Two weeks ago she couldn't steam milk."

Last semester I edited our college paper, and I only saw what I'd done in the final issue. Aparna, a second-year, had pitched a story on the hostel water shortage in her first week, so I said yes and pushed her hard: three rewrites, long comments, a call at midnight. By December her piece was on the front page and she was training others.
Dev joined the same week. I gave him the events column: dates, venues, names. I never asked what he wanted to write. I gave him fewer notes because there wasn't much to comment on. In our last meeting he said, "Yogesh bhaiya, I think I'm just not a writer."
I had decided that for him in week one. This term, every junior gets one real story and the same red pen.

qa.q: How does Dev see himself after months on the events column?
qa.a: Dev has started to believe he is "just not a writer", reading the lack of challenge as proof of low ability.

grounding: Illustrates a mentor looking back and seeing that the junior given a demanding story grew while the one kept on routine listings lost confidence.

Monday: Lalremsiami got the call for the analyst interview and told her flatmate Indu, "They'll pick someone from a bigger college. No point." She opened the company's annual report, read one page and closed it.
Thursday: In the interview room her hands were cold. When the panel asked about the company's last quarter, she said, "Sorry, I didn't get to that," and her voice went thin. She kept apologising after every answer and stared at the table.
Saturday: The rejection email came. "See? I knew," she told Indu, sounding almost relieved. Indu, folding clothes, said quietly, "You also read one page, Siami." Lalremsiami didn't answer. Late that night, though, she opened the report again and read it to the end.

qa.q: How many pages of the report did Lalremsiami read on Monday?
qa.a: One page.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami sound almost relieved when the rejection came?
qa.a: Being proved right eased her anxiety for a moment; the result matched the fear she already carried, so it felt oddly safe.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami try before her next interview?
qa.a: Treat the fear as a guess, not a fact, and prepare fully anyway, such as reading the whole report and practising answers aloud with Indu.

qa.q: How does Indu see what happened?
qa.a: Indu sees that thin preparation, not fate, helped cause the result, and says so gently.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose certainty of failing an interview led to little preparation and visible anxiety, then took the rejection as confirmation.

passage:
Yamini, sit. Your Ujjwal chacha has an interview story for you. I was twenty-four, applying to the cooperative bank in Indore. Three weeks before, I had already decided I would fail. "Those boys from the city colleges will walk in," I told my mother. So why prepare? I played carrom every evening instead.
On the day, my collar was wet with sweat before I even sat down. The manager asked me something simple about interest, and my mind went white. I stammered and looked at the floor. When the no came, I said, "See, Amma, I told you."
She said, "You told yourself, and then you listened."
The next year I sat with the books every night. Same bank, same manager. That time, I got it. So, what are you doing this evening?

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do every evening instead of preparing?
qa.a: He played carrom every evening.

qa.q: What was young Ujjwal feeling when he sat down for the interview?
qa.a: He was very anxious, sweating before he sat and going blank, because he had expected failure for weeks.

qa.q: What choice turned things around for Ujjwal the next year?
qa.a: He sat with the books every night instead of assuming he would lose, so he walked in prepared.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal's mother see that he missed?
qa.a: She saw that his own prediction shaped his lack of effort: he had told himself he would fail and then acted on it.

grounding: An elder recalls how his conviction that he would fail an interview led him to skip preparation, freeze and fail, then treat it as proof.

I'm Keerthana, and three months into the new job I caught myself forecasting again. Before the team lunch I thought, "They're a tight group. I'll sit there invisible." Last year that thought would have kept me quiet all afternoon.
This time I treated it like a guess to test. I walked in and spoke first: I asked Lalit, who had just joined from Kochi, how his flat hunt was going. Two others joined in with tips about brokers. It wasn't magic; one person barely looked up. But that night I wrote it down as evidence: four conversations, one cold shoulder.
Lalit presents his first report next week. I've decided to expect something good from him too, and to tell him clearly what to fix if it isn't.

passage:
Monday: The maths test came back. Abhinav had 9 out of 25 and Pradeep had 8. Abhinav crumpled his paper. "I'm stupid at maths. Always will be." Pradeep frowned at his. "I didn't do the fractions chapter. That's why."
Wednesday: Miss announced a retest on Friday. Pradeep practised fractions at recess, muttering under his breath. Abhinav drew cricket bats on his rough page. "Why bother? I'll fail again."
Friday: Pradeep got 17. Abhinav got 10 and stared out of the window. "Told you," he said. Pradeep pushed his rough page across. "Try the fractions ones with me tomorrow. That's the part you missed too."

qa.q: What mark did Pradeep get on Friday?
qa.a: Pradeep got 17.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he said "Why bother? I'll fail again"?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and discouraged, sure that being "stupid at maths" could never change.

qa.q: What could help Abhinav try again?
qa.a: Seeing the problem as one chapter rather than himself, and practising fractions with Pradeep as offered.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's explanation of his low mark change what he does?
qa.a: Because Pradeep blamed a chapter he skipped, the problem felt fixable, so he practised and improved.

grounding: Shows two children explaining the same bad test differently, one as a permanent flaw and one as a missed chapter, and how that shapes whether they try again.

passage:
Arre, one bad test and your face looks like a burnt roti? Listen. When I was in class four in Lucknow, your Dilnaz Nani failed the dictation test. So did my best friend Aditi. I cried under the neem tree and told her, "I am stupid. I'll never learn spellings."
Aditi wiped her nose and said, "I didn't practise the long words, that's all." Every evening that week she wrote ten hard words on her slate. I didn't. Why bother, if I was stupid?
Next test, she got nearly all of them right. I failed again, and believed it even more. Only in class six, when a teacher made me practise with Aditi, did I learn I wasn't stupid. I was unpractised. Now, which chapter did you skip?

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz cry after failing the dictation test?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel after the failed dictation?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hopeless, believing she was stupid and could never learn spellings.

qa.q: What choice in the story made Aditi's next test go better?
qa.a: Aditi blamed the unpractised long words, not herself, so she wrote ten hard words on her slate each evening.

qa.q: How did Aditi see the same failed test?
qa.a: As a temporary gap in practice she could fix, not a sign that she was stupid.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how she and a friend explained the same failed test, one as being stupid and one as lack of practice, and how that shaped their next try.

"I topped the viva. And I passed biochem, which everyone says is harder."

Jasleen pulled up the question paper. "I spent forty minutes on one staining question and left three blank. That's not dumb. That's time."
"So is it forever?"
"No. The supplementary is in July." She drew a clock in the margin. "One change: full papers with a timer. Every Sunday."
"Can I say something nice now?"
"One thing."
"You just did in five minutes what would take me a week."

qa.q: How long did Jasleen spend on one staining question?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Jasleen want when asking Vinita not to say anything nice yet?
qa.a: Jasleen felt raw and wanted honesty, not comfort, because forced cheer would have felt dismissive of the disappointment.

qa.q: What one change did Jasleen choose, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Timed full papers every Sunday, because the facts showed a time problem, not a lack of ability.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel watching Jasleen argue with the inner critic?
qa.a: Vinita probably feels relieved and impressed, seeing Jasleen move from "too dumb" to a clear plan 🙂

grounding: Shows a student questioning a harsh self-judgement after failing, checking evidence and other explanations, and settling on one change rather than forced cheer.

passage:
I'm Kunal, and last month I watched two colleagues face the same launch in very different ways. Three days before our app went live, the load tests were failing. Imran kept smiling. "Everything will be fine, yaar. Good vibes only." He skipped the risk meeting to order a cake.
Joyeeta was hopeful too; she kept saying we could make it. But she stayed back, listed the three likeliest failures and set up a simple waiting page in case traffic spiked.
Launch day, traffic spiked. The site slowed to a crawl, and Joyeeta's waiting page kept customers from seeing errors. Imran looked stunned.
What I took from watching them: hope isn't the problem. Hope with no plan is.

qa.q: What did Joyeeta set up in case traffic spiked?
qa.a: A simple waiting page.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel watching the two colleagues before launch?
qa.a: Kunal seems uneasy about Imran's breezy cheer and reassured by Joyeeta's careful hope, since only one of them was getting ready.

qa.q: What could Imran learn from Joyeeta?
qa.a: He can stay hopeful while also attending the risk meeting and planning for what might go wrong.

qa.q: How might Joyeeta see Imran's "good vibes only"?
qa.a: She might find it frustrating, since his cheer skipped the work that actually protected customers.

grounding: A colleague observes one person insisting all will be fine while ignoring failing tests, and another who stays hopeful but plans, and sees which one helps.

passage:

For the record, since we'll plan this again next year. The forecast showed heavy rain for Saturday evening. qa.a: A short "what could go wrong" list, so optimism comes with preparation, as Mr Thomas's backup did.

qa.q: What was it like for Lavanya when the speakers stopped?
qa.a: She was upset and near tears, having promised everyone it would be perfect and left the sound system uncovered.

grounding: A coordinator's note contrasts a colleague who dismissed the rain risk with one who hoped for the best but booked a backup, and learns from the difference.

passage:
Wednesday, late.
Grant results tomorrow. The office felt like two different weather systems today.
Sanjeev kept saying, "Chill, we're definitely getting it, the universe owes us." When I asked what happens to the girls' evening classes if we don't, he laughed: "Vandana, you think too much."
Bhavna is just as hopeful, maybe more; she believes our proposal is strong. But she has also sent a smaller request to two other funders and listed which classes we keep going if we get less. She said, "I want it badly. That's why I've planned for a no."
Honestly, Sanjeev's cheer made me more nervous and Bhavna's list made me calmer. Strange. Whatever happens tomorrow, I know whose plan I'm following.

qa.q: How many other funders did Bhavna send a smaller request to?
qa.a: Two other funders.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel around each colleague?
qa.a: Vandana felt more nervous around Sanjeev's cheer and calmer around Bhavna's list, because only one of them had faced the risk.

qa.q: How could Sanjeev keep his optimism and still be responsible?
qa.a: Keep hoping, but take Vandana's question seriously and help plan for the evening classes if the grant falls through.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see hope and planning?
qa.a: For Bhavna they go together: wanting the grant badly is exactly why she planned for a no.

grounding: A colleague's diary contrasts one co-worker's carefree certainty with another's hope backed by preparation, and notes which one steadies the team.

passage:
Reading-room note, Tuesday. Librarian, district library.
Manoj, a regular, got his exam result at the desk this morning and put his head down on the table. His friend Urmila, who studies in the next row, came and sat beside him. She didn't tell him to cheer up. For nearly half an hour she mostly listened while he said three years were wasted.
Then she took a sheet and drew a line down it. On one side: the result, the years gone. On the other: his strong essay marks, the optional subject he could change, whether to try once more at all. She asked, "What's one thing for this week?" He wrote: "Talk to my old teacher about the optional."
They left together at five. I kept his usual seat for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Manoj write as his one thing for this week?
qa.a: Talk to my old teacher about the optional.

qa.q: What did Urmila want when she chose not to tell Manoj to cheer up?
qa.a: She wanted him to feel heard; she cared enough to sit with his disappointment before trying to fix anything.

qa.q: Why does Urmila's two-sided sheet help?
qa.a: It separates what is fixed, like the result, from what can change, like the optional subject, so one small step becomes visible.

qa.q: What was it like for Manoj to be listened to for half an hour?
qa.a: He likely felt less alone and less defeated, able to move from "three years wasted" to a single task.

grounding: A librarian's note shows a young adult listening to a friend's despair without dismissing it, then sorting fixed from changeable and finding one next step.

passage:
Friday night.
Alka called at 9, crying. Third rejection for her paper. "Nitin, please don't tell me everything happens for a reason." So I didn't. I let her talk for a long time: two years of work, a supervisor who barely replies, feeling like the only one in the lab who can't do it. I said it sounded exhausting, and I meant it.
Later, when she'd gone quiet, I asked if we could sort it into two piles. Can't change: the rejection, the two years. Can change: the methods section the reviewer flagged, which journal she tries next, how she asks her supervisor for time.
She picked one: email her supervisor on Monday asking for twenty minutes. Small. But her voice sounded different when we hung up.

qa.q: What time did Alka call?
qa.a: At 9.

qa.q: What might Nitin have been feeling while letting Alka talk?
qa.a: Nitin was likely concerned and patient, caring more about Alka feeling heard than about fixing things fast.

qa.q: What does sorting things into two piles achieve?
qa.a: It separates what is fixed from what can change, so Alka can choose one doable step instead of facing everything at once.

qa.q: How did the call change things for Alka?
qa.a: Her voice sounded different by the end; with one small step chosen, she likely felt a little more hopeful and less stuck.

grounding: Shows a young adult hearing out a friend's despair without platitudes, then helping separate what is fixed from what can change and choose one small step.

passage:
"Ow! Waaah!" Anirban had bumped his head on the table.
Aadhya stopped stacking cups. She stared at him. Her lip wobbled. "Waaah!"
"Arre, Aadhya, you're not hurt, are you?" Mummy asked, picking her up.
"Ani cry," Aadhya sobbed, pointing.

qa.q: What did Anirban bump his head on?
qa.a: He bumped his head on the table.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya start crying though she wasn't hurt?

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Aadhya settle?
qa.a: She picked Aadhya up, named what was happening and showed her Ani being held.

qa.q: How might Anirban's mother see Aadhya's tears?

passage:
Creche note, Diwali week. Kavitha, room caregiver.
A cracker burst outside during snack time. Avni jumped and began to cry. Within a minute three other toddlers were crying or staring at her with worried faces; none of them had looked at the window.
I sat on the mat, took Avni on my lap and hummed our tidy-up song. The others crawled close. Soon they were quiet again.
This week we will draw the curtains and play soft music during cracker hours.

qa.q: What happened outside during snack time?
qa.a: A cracker burst outside.

qa.q: What were the other toddlers feeling when Avni began to cry?
qa.a: They felt worried and upset, catching Avni's distress though none of them had noticed the noise.

qa.q: What could help the room during cracker hours this week?
qa.a: Drawing the curtains and playing soft music, as Kavitha planned, and staying calm and close when one child cries.

qa.q: What was it like for Avni when the cracker burst?
qa.a: It was sudden and frightening; being held and hearing a familiar song helped her feel safe again.

grounding: A caregiver's festival-week note shows one toddler's crying spreading to others who did not know what had upset her.

passage:
It was harvest week, and every mother in the village was out in the paddy fields. At the anganwadi, little Lakshmi watched her Amma walk away down the mud path and let out a long wail.
Across the mat, a boy with a rattle stopped shaking it. His face crumpled. Then two more toddlers joined in, looking around, not knowing why.
Manjula, the helper, scooped Lakshmi up and sat down among them, clapping softly and singing the harvest song. One by one the cries turned into sniffles.

qa.q: Where were the mothers during harvest week?
qa.a: Every mother in the village was out in the paddy fields.

qa.q: What was the boy with the rattle feeling when Lakshmi wailed?
qa.a: He felt upset and uneasy, catching Lakshmi's sadness without knowing why she cried.

qa.q: How did Manjula help the whole group settle?
qa.a: She held Lakshmi and sat among all of them, clapping softly and singing, so calm could spread instead.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's Amma feel if she heard the crying from the path?
qa.a: She might feel torn and worried, needing to work in the fields yet wanting to comfort her child.

grounding: Shows one toddler's wail at a village anganwadi spreading to other toddlers who do not know why they are crying.
